description: Functions, arrow functions, scope and closures.

questions.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
What does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.answer:
It returns undefined implicitly. The value undefined is also returned when return is written with no expression after it.

code:
function noop() {}
console.log(noop());  // undefined

real example:
Map callbacks that forget a return produce undefined entries, so a map over locator texts without a return yields an array of undefined values.

questions.question: What are default parameters and how do they behave with undefined?
questions.answer:
Default parameters kick in only when the argument is undefined or omitted, not when it is null. They let functions support optional configuration.

code:
function wait(ms = 1000) { return ms; }
console.log(wait());         // 1000
console.log(wait(undefined)); // 1000
console.log(wait(null));      // null

real example:
Playwright helper functions with defaults like a standard timeout make tests readable when the caller only overrides some options.

What is the difference between arrow functions and regular functions?

What is a closure?
What is the difference between global scope, function scope, and block scope?
What is an IIFE and why is it used?
What is a higher-order function?
What is a callback function?
What is callback hell and how is it solved?
questions.answer:
Callback hell is deeply nested asynchronous callbacks that become unreadable and hard to debug. It is solved by promises chaining with then and finally by async/await.

code:
apiCall(data)
  .then(r => apiCall2(r))
  .then(r2 => apiCall3(r2));

real example:
Sequential API setup for login, then item creation, then checkout reads top to bottom with await instead of five levels of nesting.

questions.question: How do you handle a variable number of arguments without rest parameters?
What does it mean that functions are first-class citizens in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and manipulated like any other value.

code:
const fn = function () { return 1; };
const runner = f => f() + 1;
console.log(runner(fn));  // 2

real example:
Passing a polling predicate like page.waitForFunction(myCheck) naturalizes assertions as plain function values.
